raw_text:
The clinical management of coronary artery disease has undergone a series of revolutionary milestones, progressing from plain balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and, subsequently, to drug-eluting stents (DES). While contemporary metallic DES have dramatically reduced restenosis and acute vessel closure, they permanently cage the coronary vessel. This persistent footprint restricts natural vasomotion, hinders late expansive remodeling, and exposes patients to a lifelong risk of very late stent thrombosis [21, 30]. To address these drawbacks, the concept of "vascular restoration therapy" was introduced, employing temporary bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) designed to provide mechanical support and drug delivery during the initial healing phase before undergoing complete bioresorption [24, 28].

The first-generation Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular), constructed from a poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) backbone, pioneered this field. Early clinical feasibility was established in first-in-human studies, demonstrating vascular restoration and favorable long-term outcomes at 10 years [1, 2, 26]. Short-term clinical outcomes in early randomized trials, such as ABSORB II [3] and the ABSORB STEMI TROPHI II trial [25], initially supported the safety of these polymeric scaffolds, showing comparable outcomes to metallic DES in highly selected lesions.

However, as these clinical trials progressed to mid- and long-term follow-up, concerning safety signals emerged. Large randomized controlled trials, notably ABSORB III [4] and the AIDA trial [8], revealed significantly higher rates of target lesion failure (TLF) and scaffold thrombosis (ScT) with the Absorb BVS compared to contemporary cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (CoCr-EES) [6, 9]. Patient-level pooled meta-analyses confirmed these findings, indicating a two- to three-fold higher risk of both early and late ScT with BVS [5, 7, 18, 19, 29]. The elevated hazard of very late scaffold thrombosis led to a major clinical setback [10], culminating in the commercial withdrawal of the Absorb BVS and a subsequent Class III recommendation ("not recommended") in clinical practice guidelines [20].

Pathophysiological evaluations and intravascular imaging, particularly high-resolution optical coherence tomography (OCT) [23], identified several mechanical and procedural contributors to these adverse events [12]. First-generation polymeric scaffolds possessed thick struts (~150 µm) to maintain sufficient radial strength, which disrupted laminar blood flow, delayed endothelialization, and increased platelet activation [22, 30]. Furthermore, suboptimal implantation techniques frequently led to incomplete scaffold expansion, malapposition, and strut fracture [12].

To mitigate these risks, clinical consensus documents emphasized the critical importance of a meticulous implantation protocol [13]. This technique, codified as "PSP" (diligent lesion Preparation, accurate vessel Sizing, and high-pressure Post-dilatation with non-compliant balloons), was shown to drastically reduce ScT rates [11, 14]. Indeed, when the PSP protocol and strict vessel sizing criteria were prospectively applied in the large-scale ABSORB IV trial, 1-year rates of ScT and TLF were significantly lower than in previous studies, narrowing the safety gap with metallic DES [22].

Despite the limitations of first-generation polymeric BVS, the underlying therapeutic concept remains highly attractive, driving the development of next-generation bioresorbable devices. These advanced technologies focus on thinner struts, improved radial strength, and optimized degradation kinetics to enhance safety. Metallic-based bioresorbable scaffolds represent a major pathway of innovation. The magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold (Biotronik) features a fast-resorbing backbone (degraded within 12 months) and thinner struts, yielding high procedural success and low TLF rates in the BIOSOLVE-II first-in-man trial [15, 16]. This safety profile has been confirmed in larger real-world populations within the BIOSOLVE-IV registry [27]. In parallel, novel polymer formulations have been introduced, such as the Fantom desaminotyrosine polycarbonate-based sirolimus-eluting scaffold, which offers thinner struts (125 µm), radiopacity, and favorable 12-month outcomes in the FANTOM II trial [17].

In conclusion, while first-generation PLLA-based BVS suffered from design limitations and suboptimal implantation techniques that led to increased rates of scaffold thrombosis, they provided valuable insights into coronary vascular biology. The transition to next-generation scaffolds featuring thinner struts, novel biomaterials, and mandatory intravascular imaging-guided PSP implantation protocols holds promise for restoring the clinical viability of vascular restoration therapy.
